NFL to Face New Trial in Sunday Ticket Class-Action Lawsuit to Determine Financial Damages

The film, which was the first-ever Brazilian project to be supported by the Le Fonds de Dotation agnès b, a philanthropic fund created by famed fashion designer Agnès Troublé, was first conceived by the duo during the early days of the pandemic. Speaking with Variety ahead of their first screening in São Paulo, the filmmakers recall the many hoops they had to jump through in those first years of development.

“It was tricky because we first began working on the project during the pandemic, and still under the Bolsonaro government, at a time when all resources were frozen; we no longer had a Ministry of Culture and our national film fund was practically nonexistent,” says Fidalgo. “This being a road trip movie made it even harder as we couldn’t travel freely at the time, so we spent those early years heavily in development, having lengthy conversations between the two of us but also with [our producers at] Gullane and other creatives.”

As for how they decided on such a wide umbrella for a film and whether the scope of the subject ever felt daunting, Rodic says “of course,” but reiterates the “magic” of working on the project was realizing how he and Fidalgo had different perspectives on the subject but also “a strong connection.” “We shared cultural references, and we loved talking about the subject, too. It was tricky at times, but those very complications led to a very singular film.”

Fidalgo echoes that thought: “This is the very genesis of the film: how can two people who are in theory so different think the consequences of the colonial project from within their specific perspectives?”

“Yvan is a white Swiss man from the global north, I’m a Black Brazilian woman from the global south, but there are many things that unite us,” she adds. “There are also several surprising moments in the film where we upend these expectations someone might have of us.”

The film has picked up several high-profile supporters in its trajectory, including “Brainstorm” director Laís Bodanzky and Oscar-winning “I’m Still Here” helmer Walter Salles . The former is an associate producer on “The Project,” while the latter is an “ongoing supporter,” according to the filmmakers.

“Rarely have I seen the issues of colonialism and whiteness addressed with such relevance,” said Salles in a statement about the film. “It is a polyphonic, proactive, and, at the same time, incisive film. It is very well directed and edited.”

As for Bodanzky, Fidalgo recalls a long mutual admiration between herself and the director. “She saw some of my early work, when I was travelling with my first short film 10 years ago, and it was a moment of a lot of togetherness between female directors,” she recalls. “Laís already had a relationship with Gullane, which produced ‘Brainstorm’ and several other films she was a part of, so when she heard about ‘The Project’ and my next feature film with Gullane, we began talking, and she came in as a consultant.”

The next project in question is “Carnaval,” which will close a trilogy Fidalgo started with “Queen” in 2016 and continued with 2019’s “Lavender.” “Carnaval,” which is currently in development, will mark the director’s first fiction feature film and tell the story of women ahead of a carnival parade in the late ’90s.

But for now, Fidalgo is focused on sharing “The Project” with audiences alongside Rodic. Screening the film this week in São Paulo is a poignant, bittersweet moment for the duo, which sees their film gain an even greater sense of urgency as Brazil gears up for a tense second round of presidential elections between current president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, infamous for glaringly racist quotes about Brazil’s enslaving past and painful colonial history. The polls will open on this Sunday, Oct. 25.

“During the six years we spent making the film, I often worried if we missed our window,” says Fidalgo about the timing. “We felt the world had moved on, but life often surprises us, and now we see ourselves showing the film ahead of such dramatic elections that offer us not two presidential candidates but a choice between good and evil.”

Fidalgo adds that “The Project” is not just a film, “it’s a manifesto.” “We are now seeing students take to the streets in Brazil following the first round of elections, and it’s thanks to them that the left has managed to gain some traction. The film is in direct conversation with this movement; it’s a doc that brings images of the Black Lives Matter protests, which I believe to be the genesis of everything we are seeing right now in the world, in countries like France, Spain and the U.S.”

“We feel the film is coming at the right time,” she emphasizes. “We believe it will connect with audiences and that people will leave the screening room with a renewed desire to go to the streets and avoid the catastrophe of another Bolsonaro government.”

“The Project: The Myth of Colonialism’s End” is produced by Gullane, Fidalgo Produções, Globo Filmes and Canal Brasil, in association with Yvan Rodic Media. The film will be available in Brazilian theaters on Nov. 19.

article_text:
With less than two months left on the Avengers: Doomsday clock, Robert Downey Jr. and Pedro Pascal swapped sides for Halloween .

The pair traded off their MCU roles in a paired costume, with Downey dressing as Pascal’s character Mr. Fantastic and Pascal as Downey’s Dr. Doom, ahead of the movie’s Dec. 18 premiere in theaters.

“Victor. Richard. Costume swap!” Downey captioned the video on Instagram.

Related Stories

‘Avengers: Doomsday’ World Series Sneak Peek Sees Mister Fantastic Throw Out First Pitch

15 Movies & Shows To Watch Before ‘Avengers: Doomsday’

Following the events of last year’s The Fantastic Four: First Steps , Avengers: Doomsday sees the multiverse collapse, forcing heroes from multiple Earths to unite against Doctor Doom (Downey).

Also returning are Pascal as Mr. Fantastic, Vanessa Kirby as Sue Storm, Joseph Quinn as Human Torch and Ebon Moss-Bachrach as The Thing after making their MCU debut in First Steps .

Watch on Deadline

View this post on Instagram

Additionally, the cast includes Chris Hemsworth as Thor, Anthony Mackie as Captain America, Chris Evans as Steve Rogers, Paul Rudd as Ant-Man, Tenoch Huerta as Namor, Simu Liu as Shang-Chi, Letitia Wright as Black Panther, Kelsey Grammer as Beast, Danny Ramirez as Falcon, Winston Duke as M’Baku, Tom Hiddleton as Loki, Patrick Stewart as Professor X, Ian McKellen as Magneto, Alan Cumming as Nightcrawler, Rebecca Romijn as Mystique, James Marsden Cyclops, Channing Tatum Gambit and more.

News

Weekly News Roundup: November 6, 2026

INHWA YEOM’s

Chandra Chronicles: In Neuroverse , 2025–26, at “AS _____ AS POSSIBLE,” Centre Pompidou Hanwha, Seoul, 2026. Copyright the Hanwha Foundation of Culture. Courtesy the Centre Pompidou Hanwha.

Centre Pompidou Hanwha Unveils Commissions Backed by AI Giant Anthropic

Anthropic, the American AI giant behind Claude, has supported five new commissions currently on display at Seoul’s Centre Pompidou Hanwha, marking the company’s first cultural partnership in South Korea. On view through November 13, the commissioned works by MinOhrichar, Inhwa Yeom, Ubac Studio, Kahee Jeong, and Mirim Chu, are part of the group exhibition “AS _____ AS POSSIBLE,” spanning video, sound, and interactive installations. The collaboration started out as a forum, dubbed the Seoul Research Salon, which explored the mechanisms of AI systems. Speaking with Ocula, Jieun Seo, senior curator at the Hanwha Foundation of Culture, said that rather than “tak[ing] a definitive position for or against AI,” the show “aims to create an open space in which artists and audiences can reflect on what technology makes possible.” The project raises concerns about AI corporations becoming involved with museums, and comes amid Anthropic’s controversial acquisition of Korean books to train its language model. Moreover, prior to the Centre Pompidou Hanwha’s opening in June, 100-plus French artists, researchers, and art professionals petitioned to boycott the institution over Hanwha Group’s ties to Israeli arms manufacturers.

Workers at 61st Venice Biennale Join Global Dockworkers’ Strike

On October 30, cultural workers and artists at the Venice Biennale went on strike in solidarity with global protests against the militarization of ports, rising fuel costs, and poor living and working conditions. Further coinciding with a national general strike in Italy and supported by 25-plus international unions, the action saw the partial or complete closure of around 20 national pavilions at the Venice Biennale, including those of Japan, Korea, India, and Lebanon. The dockworkers’ strikes, organized by the grassroots campaigning collective No Harbour For Genocide, further call for “an immediate end to the genocide of the Palestinian people and all imperialist wars,” as their statement reads. The 61st Venice Biennale has already been disrupted by numerous shutdowns and rallies demanding the exclusion of Israel and Russia from this year’s edition.

teamLab Announces Expansion to the US

Japanese art collective teamLab has revealed plans for its first permanent museum in the US, scheduled to open in 2030. Designed by Los Angeles-based architecture firm Smith-Clementi, the forthcoming outpost will be located within OCVIBE, a USD 5 billion mixed-use district currently under development in Anaheim, California. Though the final design and budget are still being finalized, OCVIBE CEO Bill Foltz told Artnet that “the investment we’re making is well over USD 100 million,” making it “one of the more significant investments within the OCVIBE district.” The museum will span approximately 10,200 square meters, featuring a textured exterior inspired by organic forms and responding to shifting light, and house teamLab’s immersive digital installations, though further details about the inaugural exhibition are yet to be announced. The project marks teamLab’s latest international expansion. Founded in 2001, the Japanese art collective has established permanent venues in Tokyo, Osaka, Kyoto , Abu Dhabi, and Jeddah, showcasing interactive installations exploring the relationship between nature, technology, and human perception.

MELATI SURYODARMO at the 13th Nandur Srawung, Yogyakarta, 2026. Courtesy Nandur Srawung.

Melati Suryodarmo Wins 2026 Nandur Srawung Lifetime Achievement Award

On October 27, Indonesian performance artist Melati Suryodarmo received the Lifetime Achievement Award from the 13th edition of Nandur Srawung, an art exhibition held annually at the Taman Budaya Yogyakarta. Renowned for her physically demanding, hours-long performances that draw on traditional Javanese dance to explore themes of love, labor, and memory, Suryodarmo was honored for her significant contributions to the Indonesian contemporary art scene. Upon receiving the award, Suryodarmo gave an address in which she emphasized that artistic expression is “a way of living and continuing to open oneself to things not yet understood,” inviting audiences to continue supporting experimentation and creative freedom.
excerpt_original: Centre Pompidou Hanwha unveils Anthropic-backed commissions, Venice Biennale cultural workers go on strike, teamLab expands to the US, and more. The Editors

Artist Sneaks His Work Into the Met Museum

David Mitlaski says his oil pastel painting of the Met Gala captures “A-list celebrities prancing, while the world outside the museum gates is collapsing.”

Hyperallergic via

Amid the spate of publicized museum heists sweeping the globe, one Los Angeles artist has flipped the script by adding his own artwork to the walls of New York's Metropolitan Museum of Art.

In a viral Instagram reel , multi-hyphenate artist David (Sabastian) Miklatski detailed the steps of creating and surreptitiously installing a drawing on one of The Met's gallery walls last Sunday, October 25.

The work in question, “The MET 2027,” is an oil pastel painting depicting a Met Gala attendee ascending the staircase flanked by shrubs and photojournalists as police in riot gear beat down protestors in a fiery scene in the foreground.

In the video, Miklatski juxtaposes clips of stars like Zendaya and Sabrina Carpenter getting photographed at the Met Gala with footage of mining conditions in the Congo, riots in Paris and Milan, homelessness in the United States, the US- and Israeli-led mutilation of Gaza, gang violence in Haiti, and Russia bombing Ukraine.

Capturing the “absurdity of it all,” Miklatski says the painting depicts “A-list celebrities prancing, while the world outside the museum gates is collapsing.”

article_text:
Art Review

How Mexican Photographers Made a Nation

A show at the Getty demonstrates the way modernist approaches to photography shifted the visual culture of Mexico in the 20th century.

Hyperallergic )

LOS ANGELES — In “Tríptico de los martirios” (1950), the late photographer Lola Álvarez Bravo patiently renders her subject anonymous, capturing a tree’s shadow crawling toward her subject’s bare chest with exquisite timing. In Graciela Iturbide’s “Mujer ángel” (1979), meanwhile, a woman with a veil, long white skirt, and portable stereo traverses a field of flowers to encounter a spotty desert. Almost cinematic in their presentation, both works demonstrate a keen attention to light and form as well as an emotional sensitivity to their subjects, demonstrating the way modernist approaches to photography shifted the visual culture of Mexico in the 20th century.

The work of both artists is prominently featured in Instante/revelación: Moments in Mexican Photography at the Getty Center in Los Angeles, which brings together the work of 13 Mexican photographers from the late 1920s to the mid-2010s to trace the arc from post-Revolution nation-building to contemporary life through photography.

Instante/revelación: Moments in Mexican Photography

The exhibition takes its name from a book published by the late Nobel Prize-winning Mexican writer Octavio Paz entitled Instante y revelación (Instant and Revelation, 1982). In it, Paz pairs his poetry with photographs by Manuel Álvarez Bravo, whose work he encountered in the Mexican literary magazine Contemporáneos (Contemporaries) . This relationship between language and visual art informs the exhibition’s framework, allowing for poetic groupings. In this way, artists and intellectuals, including Frida Kahlo, Diego Rivera, and David Alfaro Siqueiros, are shown alongside landscapes, botanical species, and scenes from everyday life.

article_text:
E arly this summer, in a pristine, limestone mountain range in the East Java province of Indonesia, Mohammad Nur Nasikin met with the father and son pictured here. His aim was to capture a character from a treasured Indonesian theatrical dance and art form called Reog Ponorogo.

“Bujang Ganong is one of the characters in the dance; a young regent who is agile, skilful and clever,” Nasikin explains, “Mr Hanafie, on the left, is a true artist, skilled in many Javanese arts. He’s wearing the traditional costume worn by a Bujang Ganong dancer: a wooden ganong mask, and a bright red waistcoat, a shoulder cloth known as a sembong, and loose‑fitting trousers called katok panji. At his feet is his drummer – his son Tirta, which means ‘water’ in Javanese.”

The energetic movements of the character made it easy to capture a range of shots, Nasikin notes. When he returned home, Nasikin showed his own 12-year-old son, and explained the importance of preserving culture passed from ancestors.

“We must continue to safeguard it for generations to come,” he says. “My hope is that viewers will be interested in learning more about this art form, and our culture, and in that way I will have formed a link between the past and the future.”
